idea.why: A genuine three-role crew with an explicit instruction that the merger adds nothing of its own. Having the model emit structured data while a deterministic node emits markup is exactly the seam a knowledgeable designer would cut. Reservations: the decomposition implies two independent specialists but realises them one after the other.

structure.why: Right node types and a proportionate count. Two small misfits: the merger has no tools, so it is an Agent doing a chain's job, and both fetch tools are pinned to fixed queries described as taking no arguments, which spends a model round-trip on a deterministic fetch.

connections.why: Sub-node wiring is right. The main chain is the weak part: the calendar agent waits on the inbox agent only so it can be reached by reference later. The textbook serialised-unrelated-fetches shape, and a Gmail failure silently takes the calendar leg with it.

answer.why: End to end it does what was asked, in inline-styled table-laid-out HTML that survives a mail client, with escaping and per-section empty states. What keeps it off the top band is presentation as email only, and a send target left blank so the first run needs a manual fill.

appraisal: Finds the right shape for a daily briefing: specialists that gather and interpret, a merger that ranks, and a deterministic renderer so no model is asked to produce markup. The HTML is the standout, email-safe inline styles, escaped values, count tiles and real empty states, and the structured schema means a bad generation degrades to empty sections instead of broken output. The clear weakness is the wiring: independent work chained in series purely so the merger can reach the first agent by reference, which both fakes a dependency and couples two failure paths. A knowledgeable user would fan both analysts out and rejoin with a Merge, then demote the merger from an Agent to a chain since it holds no tools.
